dog.now.why: Personal a: a known animal as object takes a, so the dog is al perro. No yo: the -o on tengo que already says I.

dog.past.why: Two different pasts: quería (imperfect) for the wish, tuve que (preterite) because the hiding really happened.

dog.neg.why: No do-support: each no sits right before its verb. No tengo que means no need, exactly like don't have to.

dog.q.why: The ¿ opens mid-sentence, right where the question part starts. Same order as a statement; the -es on tienes marks tú.

cant.now.why: Car keys becomes las llaves del carro (keys of the car): Spanish does not stack nouns. Ir, not venir, for going to their place.

cant.past.why: pudimos (preterite) holds we, can and past in one word, so couldn't needs no helper: just no in front.

cant.fut.why: Like English, the future splits can: vamos a poder (going to be able to). No podremos ir is the more written option.

cant.although.why: Still becomes fronted igual (anyway), everyday Latin American speech. aunque + indicative escondieron states a real fact.

like.now.why: Flipped: literally coffee pleases my sister. A mi hermana names the liker, le repeats it, and gusta agrees with el café.

like.neg.why: no goes right before le, never between le and gusta. A ella is optional, but le alone could also mean him or usted.

like.they.why: Two parents, yet gusta stays singular because coffee is the subject; only le becomes les. Papás is the everyday word for parents.

like.q.why: te marks tú as the liker; the words match a statement and only intonation and ¿? make it a question. No do.

go.habit.why: a + el fuses into al, so al mercado moves as one unit. Every Sunday is todos los domingos: all the Sundays, plural.

go.prog.why: Plain present van covers are going; ahora mismo pins it to now. Ahorita is avoided: in Mexico it can mean in a while.

go.past.why: fueron packs they, go and past into one word. It is also the preterite of ser, so alone it can mean they were.

go.fut.why: van a ir, go-to-go: the future sits on van a and ir repeats as the infinitive. Mañana van al mercado is just as common.

go.neg.why: No aux, no -ing: no before plain present van says they aren't going. English aren't does two jobs; Spanish splits them.

live.now.why: Present vive, not a perfect: desde hace dos años (since it makes two years) carries the still-true meaning.

live.past.why: No él: the -ó ending says he and past. The finished stretch is bare dos años, with no word for for.

live.fut.why: No future perfect in speech: va a cumplir (going to complete) carries the tense, viviendo the verb. Habrá vivido sounds written.

live.q.why: llevar + gerund is the spoken have-been-ing: llevas holds tú and the ongoing time, viviendo the verb.

rain.now.why: No it: weather verbs take no subject, so está lloviendo starts bare. llévate is the tú command with -te glued on.

rain.fut.why: va a llover mirrors going to rain, minus the it. Más tarde moves to the front, which sounds more natural than at the end.

rain.neg.why: The negative order changes form: llévate becomes no lleves (subjunctive), and -te drops. Paraguas goes bare, with no un.

if.real.why: si + present, then ir a + infinitive. Viajaremos or plain viajamos are also heard. Never a future right after si.

if.unreal.why: Four words: tuviéramos (imperfect subjunctive) after si, and the -íamos ending on viajaríamos does the job of we would.

if.past.why: Both halves use haber + participle. In speech hubiéramos viajado often replaces habríamos in the second half too.
